title: Risk and return go together
summary: See why higher possible gains come with higher chance of loss.

variants.markdown:
**English draft for R5 review.**

Kabir and Tara each have ₹1,000 of play money. Kabir keeps his in a steady savings idea that grows slowly, around an assumed 5% a year. Tara tries a risky idea that might give 15% in a good year, or lose 10% in a bad one. These numbers are **an assumption for this example, not a promise**.

That is the **risk-return trade-off**. Choices with a higher chance of big gains also have a higher chance of losses. **Risk** means the outcome can vary, and the result may be less than you hoped.

No one can tell the future, so a high past return never guarantees a high future one.

One way to handle risk is **diversification**: not putting all your money in one place. If one part falls, others may hold up. It lowers the damage of any single bad outcome, but it cannot remove risk completely.

Ask: how much loss could I accept, and for how long?

Gullak uses virtual play money only.

questions.prompt: What usually comes with a chance of higher returns?
questions.explanation: Higher possible returns generally come with higher risk.

options.text: Putting all money in one choice

questions.explanation: Spreading money helps reduce the damage from any one bad outcome.

questions.prompt: A choice gave 15% last year. What does this tell us?

options.text: It does not guarantee the future

questions.explanation: Past returns do not promise future ones; every choice carries uncertainty.
